title: Should Teachers Explain or Demonstrate?
author: Watson, Andrew
source: Learning and the Brain Blog (learningandthebrain.com), May 28, 2023
summary: Andrew Watson reports on a 2023 study (Sumers, Ho, Hawkins & Griffiths) that tested whether explaining a strategy in words or demonstrating it by example produces better learning between strangers solving an online puzzle. The finding depended on complexity: for simple puzzles, showing and telling worked equally well, but for complex puzzles, telling outperformed showing. A follow-up experiment tested whether this held for abstract versus concrete content and found that words specifically outperform demonstration when the content being taught is abstract rather than concrete. Watson is careful to flag the study's limits, since it involved adult strangers rather than trained teachers and a maze-solving task far removed from typical classroom content, before drawing a cautious teaching implication anyway: that precise, rehearsed language matters more than teachers with years of experience tend to assume, especially for abstract concepts. He connects the finding to Oliver Caviglioli's work on dual coding, noting that this study pushes him to take the "telling" half of dual coding as seriously as the "showing" half, particularly for abstract material like the concept of checkmate in chess.
points: Watson's key finding-to-classroom bridge is that language becomes more important, not less, as the concept being taught becomes more abstract, since demonstration alone increasingly fails to transmit abstract rules.

He explicitly resists overclaiming from the study, listing three specific ways the experimental task (adult strangers, no teaching expertise, maze-solving) differs from real classroom teaching before drawing any implication.
His personal takeaway is a discipline of scripting and rehearsing explanations in advance, pushing back against the temptation of experienced teachers to "wing it" on concepts they know well.

He reframes dual coding through this study, arguing that teachers, including himself, tend to over-focus on the "showing/drawing" half and underweight the "telling" half, especially for abstract content.
quotes: Our findings suggest that language communicates complex concepts by directly transmitting abstract rules. In contrast, demonstrations transmit examples, requiring the learner to infer the rules.
For simple puzzles, both methods worked equally well. For complex puzzles, telling helped more than showing.
Because this research differs A LOT from typical classroom work, its findings might not apply precisely to classroom work.
That is: when I’m explaining a concept to my students for the first time, I should script and rehearse my explanation carefully.
This study, however, reminds me that the “telling” part is equally important — and, in the case of highly abstract concepts, might even be more important.
